html:
The great temple complex of the god Amun at Thebes, now Luxor, in Egypt. Kings added to it for about two thousand years, from Senusret I around 1970 BCE to the Ptolemies, which made it one of the largest religious sites ever built.

Most of what stands dates from the New Kingdom, when Thebes was the capital and Amun the chief god. Each king built a new gate, court or hall in front of the last:

  • Hatshepsut raised obelisks of red granite, one still standing about 30 metres high;
  • the Great Hypostyle Hall, finished under Ramesses II, has 134 columns, the central ones 21 metres tall;
  • an avenue of sphinxes ran about 3 km south to the temple of Luxor.

The priests of Amun grew rich on land and gifts and came to rival the kings. Akhenaten closed the temple for a time in favour of his sun god; it was reopened after his death.
